# Load Cellranger count

```{r,message=FALSE}
library(SingleCellExperiment)

# Load 10x dataset
o <- DropletUtils::read10xCounts("filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5")
o <- splitAltExps(o,rowData(o)$Type,ref = "Gene Expression")
```


```{r,message=FALSE}
# Add genes annotations
rowData(o) <- cbind(
  rowData(o),
  local({
    meta <- read.table("../01_genome/mouse/data/gene_info.tsv",sep="\t",header=TRUE)
    meta[match(rowData(o)$ID,meta$ensembl_gene_id),]
  })
)
#rowData(o)$go_ids <- CharacterList(strsplit(rowData(o)$go_ids,";"))
```



# Introduction


## HDF5 format
CellRanger store gene expression matrices into files with `.h5` extension (`filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5`). 
This file is encoded into the standard format HDF5 (more information [here](https://www.hdfgroup.org)), which is a compressed binary format structured to allow random access to its content. In simple words, it means we can works on the data without loading everything into memory.

To work with HDF5-files, we recommend to use the Bioconductor package `rhdf5`. 
HDF5-files are organised hierarchically similarly to folders into a filesystem, and to browse their content use `rhdf5::h5ls()`.

```{r}
rhdf5::h5ls("filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5")
```

To read the content of a HDF5, one can use `rhdf5::h5read()`. This function will load all the data into memory. 
For example to load gene names from a CellRanger h5.
```{r}
head(rhdf5::h5read("filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5","/matrix/features/name"))
```


However, when the data do not fit into memory, like large gene-expression matrices, one should use `HDF5Array` package to map the content of the HDF5 file into an object that can be manipulated similarly to a matrix.
```{r}
HDF5Array::TENxMatrix("filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5","/matrix")
```



## Create SingleCellExperiment objects
`SingleCellExperiment` allows to associate metadata to gene expression counts, and then facilitate data manipulation.





# Add HTO informations (optional, only if available)

```{r}
o <- local({
  # Load HTO data
  hto <- DropletUtils::read10xCounts("filtered_feature_bc_matrix_HTO.h5")
  
  # Check overlap with gene expression
  gplots::venn(list(HTO=hto$Barcode,exp=o$Barcode));title("barcode overlap")
  
  # Remove cell with none matching barcode in the HTO
  o <- o[,o$Barcode %in% hto$Barcode]
  
  # Add HTO informations to the data
  altExp(o,"Antibody Capture") <- hto[,match(o$Barcode,hto$Barcode)]
  
  o
})
```


```{r}
# Determine 
v <- altExp(o,"Antibody Capture") |> 
  assay() |>
  as.matrix()
v <- t(v/rowMeans(v))
heatmap(log1p(v[sample(nrow(v),1000),1:11]),scale="none")

source("../lib_util.R")
i <- order.col(-v)
V <- array(v[cbind(as.vector(row(i)),as.vector(i))],dim(i))
tag <- i[,1]
tag[V[,1] - V[,2] < 1] <- 0

table(tag)
plot(sort(V[,1] - V[,2]),log="y")


```






# Add samples meta-data

When possible add the following meta-data, respecting the field names:
`sex`, `age`, `cell_type`

The field `label` is reserved for sample labeling.


# Store SingleCellExperiment object as H5AD



# Parking

H5 format is a standard format to `.h5` At this step, you should do your
best to organize your data and collect meta-data as the generated
`h5ad`-file will be used at all step of your analysis.

Using data loaded from CellRanger output, we create a
`SingleCellExperiment()` object which will store all our data and
metadata. The content of this object will be stored into the final
`h5ad` file. We try to respect specific field name conventions for
compatibility: - Use following assay names when relevant: `counts`,
`normcounts`, `logcounts`, `tpm`, `cpm` - Use gene symbol names as
rownames to easily query the object. Preserve gene identifiers into the
rowData. - Try to store genomic positions of the features as character
string into `rowData()$interval`. You will later be able to convert this
information into `GRanges()` to work with them
